final_answer:
Let \(A=k[x]/(x^{n+1})\). The relation
\[
yx=xy+x^r
\]
says that \(R_{n,r}\) is the Ore extension
\[
R_{n,r}=A[y;\delta],
\qquad \delta(x)=x^r,
\]
so
\[
ya=ay+\delta(a)\quad(a\in A).
\]
Since \(\delta(x^{n+1})=(n+1)x^{n+r}=0\) in \(A\), this is well-defined. Every element has a unique normal form
\[
z=\sum_{j=0}^m a_j(x)y^j,\qquad a_j(x)\in A.
\]

First require \(z\) to commute with \(y\). We have
\[
[y,z]=\sum_{j=0}^m \delta(a_j)y^j,
\]
so \(z\) commutes with \(y\) iff every \(a_j\in \ker\delta\). Now
\[
\delta(x^i)=i x^{i+r-1}.
\]
Because \(\operatorname{char}k=0\), this vanishes in \(A\) exactly when \(i=0\) or \(i+r-1\ge n+1\), i.e. \(i\ge n-r+2\). Thus
\[
\ker\delta
=
k\oplus (x^{\,n-r+2})\subset A.
\]

Now impose commutation with \(x\). For \(m\ge1\),
\[
[x,y^m]
\]
has leading \(y\)-degree \(m-1\) term
\[
-mx^r y^{m-1},
\]
and all its coefficients lie in the ideal \((x^r)\). Therefore, if
\[
z=\sum_{j=0}^m a_jy^j
\]
commutes with \(y\), write \(a_j=c_j+b_j\) with \(c_j\in k\) and \(b_j\in (x^{n-r+2})\). Since
\[
(x^{n-r+2})(x^r)=x^{n+2}=0,
\]
the \(b_jy^j\) terms commute with \(x\). But if some highest \(c_m\ne0\) with \(m\ge1\), then the leading term of \([x,z]\) is
\[
-mc_m x^r y^{m-1}\ne0,
\]
a contradiction. Hence \(c_j=0\) for all \(j\ge1\).

So the center consists exactly of a scalar plus arbitrary terms whose \(x\)-power is at least \(n-r+2\).

\[
\boxed{
Z(R_{n,r})
=
k\cdot 1
\;\oplus\;
\bigoplus_{j\ge0}\bigoplus_{i=n-r+2}^{n} k\,x^i y^j
}
\]

Equivalently, as an explicit subalgebra,
\[
\boxed{
Z(R_{n,r})=k+(x^{\,n-r+2})R_{n,r}.
}
\]
